working_title: Electric vs Push Trolley: How to Actually Choose the Right One for UK Walking Golfers
angle: A practical, opinionated guide that cuts through the marketing and helps a regular UK walking golfer decide between a push trolley and an electric trolley, using UK-specific factors (hilly courses, wet conditions, boot space, frequency of play) rather than generic pros/cons lists. The post argues there is no universal answer, but that asking the right questions about your own game narrows it down quickly.
research_notes:
- Core distinction: electric trolleys use a battery-powered motor so you steer but don't push; push trolleys require manual effort throughout the round
- Electric trolleys are heavier than push trolleys because of added motor and battery hardware, but the weight is less noticeable on the course since you are not pushing it
- Push trolleys generally offer more storage as standard than electric models; electric models may require accessories to match storage capacity
- For hilly UK courses, electric trolleys have a clear advantage: advanced braking systems, downhill control (e.g. Motocaddy DHC feature on several models), and powered traction
- Push trolleys better suited to flatter courses and golfers on tighter budgets
- Three-wheel push trolleys are the go-to for UK walking golfers who play on uneven or changing terrain
- Old-fashioned two-wheel pull trolleys are worth avoiding due to strain on one side of the body
- Key electric trolley buying factors for UK golfers: battery life matched to round length (18-hole, 27-hole, or 36-hole lithium options available); compact fold matters because electric trolleys are heavier to lift in and out of car boots
- Lithium batteries are lighter and last longer than older lead-acid types with normal care
- Notable UK brands: PowaKaddy (founded 1983, based in Sittingbourne, Kent; FX and CT ranges prominent in UK market), Motocaddy (S1, M1, M7 GPS Remote among key models), Stewart Golf (UK-made R1-S push trolley in aerospace-grade aluminium; Q Follow electric uses Bluetooth follow technology)
- Push trolley price reference points: PowaKaddy Micra around £189, Clicgear 4.0 around £219, Stewart R1-S at a premium above most competitors
- Electric trolley price ranges broadly: entry-level around £300-£500, mid-range around £500-£650, premium/remote/follow models (e.g. Stewart Q Follow) in the £1,600-£1,900 range — do NOT cite these as confirmed RRPs, describe only as general price tiers
- Follow/remote electric trolleys (Stewart Q Follow uses Bluetooth; Motocaddy M7 GPS Remote) represent top of the market; follow mode described as closest thing to having a caddy
- Features worth paying for on electric models: downhill control, automatic parking brake, anti-tip wheels (relevant on UK hilly links and parkland), compact fold
- Features to skip unless you will genuinely use them: GPS add-ons if you already use a separate device, remote control if you play flat courses
- Bag-trolley compatibility: trolley and bag need to work as a pair; worth checking before buying
